title: Emotional Intelligence Project - Interview with Judith Orloff
summary: A 15-page transcript of a filmed interview with Judith Orloff for an Emotional Intelligence Project. Orloff discusses her preferred term "emotional literacy" over "emotional intelligence," defines it as the ability to be aware of internal experience and respond from that awareness. She addresses gender and cultural differences in emotional expression, how organizations like American Express, Bank of America, Fleet Bank, Midas International, Ford, and GM have adopted EI, and describes her company's approach of embedding EI into management training at three levels (beginning, functional, and business managers) rather than selling it as a standalone product. She discusses creating cognitive dissonance to drive real change, the role of franchise organizations in paradigm shifts, and implementation through web-based follow-up modules. She also covers resistance from HR professionals, the connection between emotional intelligence and workplace safety, and her belief that EI is both learned and remembered.
authorship: Judith Orloff (interviewee). Interviewer is unnamed. Produced as part of an Emotional Intelligence Project (appears to be a video/film production with offstage direction).

title: Letter from the Rebbe on the Care and Education of Jewish Children with Disabilities
summary: A letter from the Lubavitcher Rebbe dated 22 Av, 5739 (1979), responding to a request for his views on the care and education of Jewish children with intellectual disabilities. The Rebbe provides detailed guidelines including: treating each case individually rather than applying group rules, starting from the premise that disabilities are temporary and improvable, avoiding exaggerated expectations while giving guarded encouragement, involving trainees in leadership roles, addressing the controversy around 'group homes' with a recommendation for individual evaluation, emphasizing the importance of Jewish education and identity for children with disabilities (not treating it as a secondary concern), and the therapeutic value of religious observance and community belonging. The letter closes with reference to the Lubavitch principle of 'Ve'ohavta Lereacha Kamocha' (Love your fellow as yourself) and a blessing to the recipient in their capacity as Regional Chairman of the Council For Mental Retardation.

title: Natural Leadership: A Core Competency of Clarity

The document defines six guiding principles: Personal Responsibility, Sharing Direct Experience, Knowing Yourself, Honoring Our Word, Being Authentic, and Applying Skillful Means, each broken into specific sub-competencies with stated benefits. Developed over 30 years of organizational participation, it positions Natural Leadership as an innate ability to do the right thing when informed by clarity, authenticity, and natural ethics.

outline.description: Explores Understanding Our True Nature (equating it with clarity, unconditional love, Buddha mind), Assuming Innocence, and Uniting Our Personal Vision with a Larger Perspective. The mastery result is natural wisdom, natural authority, and natural ethics.

title: Dissertation Critique - Nowhere Man by Tracy John Skipp
summary: Judith Orloff's academic critique of Tracy John Skipp's 2010 doctoral dissertation "Nowhere Man: Autoethnographic Reflections on Identity, Family, and Leadership" for the ELC 727 Methods Action Research course with Dr. Anna DiStefano at Fielding Graduate University. Orloff evaluates Skipp's use of autoethnography to explore leadership intimacy, his identification with Saint Francis of Assisi, his struggle with Franciscan Roman Catholic values in a university administration setting, and his three-part framework of leadership as intimacy with self, others, and developmental intimacy. The critique addresses the study's framing concepts (personalism, intimacy, fatherhood), research methods (360 assessment, interviews, reflective journaling), and data collection challenges.

outline.title: Research Methods and Data Collection

outline.title: Findings and Conclusion

Concludes that Skipp made a valuable contribution to autoethnography literature through his engaging personal narrative, despite the other methodologies feeling unclear and tedious.

title: Insight as a Core Mechanism of Mindfulness: An Action Research Project
summary: An action research project by Judith Orloff at Fielding Graduate University investigating whether insight is a core mechanism of mindfulness practice. The paper distinguishes between Western (conceptual, Jon Kabat-Zinn) and Eastern (Buddhist, non-conceptual) mindfulness approaches, focusing on the latter. It proposes a study with 20 participants using narrative inquiry methodology, including in-depth interviews, a 28-day daily email survey with four-question assessments, and focus group exit interviews. The research questions examine whether being insightful leads to deeper mindfulness, whether insight leads to beneficial behavior, and whether insight reduces blame through reduced projection. Includes a 63-question autobiography questionnaire, mobile app mockups from Orloff's organization Radical Choices, Inc., and references to her six principles of mindfulness.
authorship: Judith Orloff, Fielding Graduate University. References her organization Radical Choices, Inc. and the app DeepSee. Mentions collaboration with Doubleday (Orloff & Doubleday 2015). title: The End of Your World - Adyashanti Interview Transcript (Sounds True)
summary: A 19-page transcript of an in-depth interview between Sounds True publisher Tami Simon and spiritual teacher Adyashanti, excerpted from his book 'The End of Your World.' Topics covered include the nature of spiritual awakening as a change of perspective rather than a blissful state, the distinction between nonabiding and abiding awakening using the 'rocket ship' metaphor, the mystery of what fuels awakening, 'Velcro thoughts' and the narrowing gap between thought and seeing through it, pure feeling vs. thought-derived emotion, the gut as an intuitive sense organ, pure anger from an undivided state, the ego co-opting awakening into missionary zeal, the dangers of spiritual inflation, the inner voice as guide vs. superego, finding one's own way rather than relying on a teacher or tradition, his experience of 'final awakening' at age 32 including seeing past lives, death as the next experience of consciousness, and his teaching that 'waking up is dying.' Includes handwritten annotations throughout marking key passages.
authorship: Interview conducted by Tami Simon (Sounds True publisher) with Adyashanti. Excerpted from the book 'The End of Your World' published by Sounds True. The document includes handwritten annotations (likely by Judith Orloff or a Radical Love Foundation reader) marking passages about secondary thought patterns, pure emotions vs. duplications of thinking, and pure anger.

outline.title: Introduction and Nature of Awakening
outline.description: Sounds True presents the interview. Adyashanti describes awakening as a change of perspective where everything thought to be real is seen as a dream within the infinite expanse of emptiness.

outline.title: Gradual vs. Sudden Awakening and the Fuel Question
outline.description: Discussion of whether awakening can sneak up gradually, and the mystery of what fuel or conditions enable it. Awakening is not limited to spiritual seekers.

outline.title: Abiding Awakening, Velcro Thoughts, and Freedom
outline.description: Adyashanti discusses nonabiding vs. abiding awakening, the gap between 'sticky' thoughts and seeing through them becoming almost nonexistent, and how frustration is experienced without secondary judging thought.

outline.title: Pure Feeling vs. Thought-Derived Emotion
outline.description: Discussion of pure sensory perceptions and emotions that bypass thinking, the gut as an intuitive sense organ, consciousness filling expanses, and the body as a sensing instrument. 'Radical In-to-me-see' (radical intimacy) as the result of sharing everything about yourself. Includes handwritten annotations about pure emotions.

outline.title: Surrender, Failure, and Awakening
outline.description: Adyashanti on ego not being in control, accepting experience rather than pushing it away, transformation through failure rather than technique, and the paradox that knowing 'there is nothing I can do' is the beginning of awakening. Closes with 'What do I know for certain? Only that I am.'

outline.title: Pure Anger and Undivided Emotion
outline.description: Discussion of whether anger can come from a pure, undivided place, referencing wrathful deities in Tibetan tradition and Jesus overturning the money changers' tables.

outline.title: Virtual Emotions and Ego Co-opting Awakening
outline.description: Adyashanti on virtual vs. real love, the cul-de-sac of missionary zeal after awakening, how ego can co-opt spiritual experience leading to inflation and delusion.

outline.title: Safeguards Against Ego Inflation and Power
outline.description: Discussion of traditional safeguards in spiritual communities, the difficulty of confronting inflated students, and Adyashanti's personal discomfort with being given power.

outline.title: The Inner Voice and Finding One's Own Way
outline.description: The still, small voice as conscience distinct from superego, its nature as guide and flow of existence, the importance of finding one's own way, and the image of cutting the cord on a spacewalk.

outline.title: Student-Teacher Relationships and Standing Alone
outline.description: How his teaching style requires students to stand on their own, the evolution from small intimate groups to larger settings, and meeting people in their sufficiency.

outline.title: Past Lives and 'Final Awakening' at Age 32

outline.title: Death, Dying, and Waking Up
outline.description: Discussion of death as the next experience consciousness has, awakening as dying ('total blankness, absolute nonexistence'), near-death experiences, and those who have let go becoming transparent to Spirit.

title: Using Nonduality to Ameliorate Early Childhood Trauma: An Autoethnography (Doctoral Dissertation, 2020)
summary: Judith Orloff's doctoral dissertation at Fielding Graduate University (Doctor of Education, 2020), chaired by Dr. Szabi Istai-Zee. An autoethnographic study exploring how early childhood trauma (emotional, physical, sexual) defines a person's future, and proposing nonduality as a foundational core therapeutic model that could be used universally alongside all modalities of therapy. The study focuses on Judith's own journey: postpartum depression and psychosis leading to misdiagnosis and psychiatric hospitalization at age 26, followed by decades of healing through nondual practice (particularly through Peter Fenner's work). Organized in five chapters: introduction and theoretical framework, literature review of nondual practitioner scholars, autoethnography as research method, a detailed personal narrative from childhood through discovering nonduality, and conclusions with a six-step nonduality-in-action process for practitioners.
authorship: Judith Orloff. Committee: Szabi Istai-Zee, PhD (Chair), Anna M. DiStefano, EdD (Research Faculty), Ira P. Glovinsky, PhD (Faculty Reader), Donna Farren (Student Reader), Alan Davis, PhD (External Examiner).

Purpose of bringing this healing model to the mainstream. Theoretical framework rooted in Fenner (2007). Discussions of conceptual vs. non-conceptual mindfulness, definition of duality, origins of nonduality across traditions (Hindu Vedanta, Buddhism, Taoism, mystical Christianity, Judaism, Islam). Use of nonduality as therapeutic modality. Significance and limitations of the study.

outline.title: Chapter Two: Review of Literature
outline.description: Four-section literature review: (1) nondual practitioner scholars and their work, (2) early childhood conditioning and its lasting effects on development, (3) mindfulness research as a precursor to nonduality and its relationship to healing trauma, (4) mentors and teachers who shaped Judith's own perspective on nonduality in action. Summary of gaps in existing literature.

outline.title: Chapter Three: Autoethnography as Method
outline.description: Overview of autoethnography as a research method for examining personal experience within social and cultural context. Description of the crucible 3-week stay at Philadelphia Psychiatric Center. Discussion of insanity, psychiatric labels, and postpartum hormone chaos in the mid-1960s. Research focus, data sources (journals, letters, class notes, many undated), a few early memories, detailed research approach, and chapter summary.

outline.title: Chapter Four: My Personal Journey — Childhood
outline.description: Opening poem 'Yearning' (free form writing, 1959, New York City). The chapter's five-section overview. Parents' troubled marriage, a loving tale with father at age 2, St. Agnes Hospital, three years old, the red mitten incident, school years ages 7-12, father's heart attack, developing as an empath, Cinderella journal entry (May 2012), trolley car memory, elementary school, private school and abuse, friend Ramona, being Jewish in Philadelphia, and taking sides as the beginning of nonduality.

outline.title: Chapter Four: My Personal Journey — Teenager through Philadelphia
outline.description: Teenage years and leaving home at 19, 1985 journal entry, moving to New York City and the beatnik era, returning to Philadelphia, Horizon House residential program (a crucible period of recovery), and University of Pennsylvania.

outline.title: Chapter Four: My Personal Journey — Vermont, Colorado, and Healing
outline.description: Vermont as a new reality, 'A Fly Cries' reflection, San Diego period, move to Colorado, marriage to soulmate, discovering nonduality and Peter Fenner through two year-long programs and 6 years of training. The last 12 years (2006-2018) weaving nondual threads into transformation from recovering mental patient to master teacher. The healing process through continually resolving trauma via nondual practice.

outline.title: Chapter Five: Now What? Conclusions and Recommendations
outline.description: Opening poem 'EXIST' (Philadelphia, 1960s). Reflections on memory as a self-woven tapestry. The research question: how does nonduality assist in ameliorating early childhood trauma? Memories shared with sister whose experience differed. Suggestions for future research, implications for practice, example of nonduality in action with a six-step process (two figures), and final reflection ending in a state of grace and appreciation.
